title: Markov Chains: Modeling Customer Journeys
subtitle: Every customer is somewhere in a journey — browsing, buying, lapsing, returning. Tonight we model those journeys as Markov chains, compute lifetime value and churn, and see how the same math built Google. Plus: MIDTERM CASE DUE — team briefings tonight.

objectives.title: Model systems with states and transition matrices
objectives.description: Represent a customer base — or any evolving system — as a set of states with transition probabilities, and use matrix multiplication to project where the population will be in one month, six months, or the long run.

objectives.title: Compute steady states and long-run behavior
objectives.description: Find the equilibrium distribution a Markov chain settles into, and understand why that single vector answers questions like 'what fraction of our customers will be active a year from now?'

objectives.title: Quantify customer lifetime value and churn
objectives.description: Turn retention and churn probabilities into dollars: compute expected customer lifetime value with absorbing states, and see why a 5-point retention improvement can be worth more than a 20-point acquisition boost.

objectives.title: Apply Markov attribution to marketing spend
objectives.description: Use the removal-effect method to credit conversions across touchpoints — the Markov-chain answer to 'did the Instagram ad or the email actually close the sale?' — and understand PageRank as the same math at web scale.

agenda.title: Where Do Customers Go?
agenda.description: Housekeeping (case submitted tonight, team briefings at 9:10), then the opening question: who has cancelled a subscription and come back? Every subscription business lives on transitions between customer states, and tonight's math prices those transitions.
bulletPoints: Tonight's rhythm: see each idea on a slide, then do it in the notebook right away
Chat vote: 80% of active customers stay each month. After a year, how many of 10,000 are left?

agenda.title: Round 1: States, the Transition Matrix & Notebook Part 1
agenda.description: The goldfish rule (the Markov property), four customer states, and one table that holds the whole story. Watch 200 customers live a year on screen, then build the same model yourself.
bulletPoints: The Markov property: next month depends only on where you are now
The transition matrix: one row per state, every row adds to 1
x @ P: everyone takes one step; a loop shows the next 36 months
Notebook Part 1: you compute the answer to the class vote (2,829)

agenda.title: Round 2: The Long Run & Notebook Part 2
agenda.description: Leave a chain running and it forgets where it started. A made-up Dunkin' vs Starbucks market shows the steady state; our subscription chain shows why a one-way door makes the long run boring and lifetime the real question.
bulletPoints: Steady state: long-run share comes from switching rates, not today's share
Absorbing states: Churned is a one-way door
Notebook Part 2: three starts meet at 66.7%; half the customers are gone by month 11

agenda.title: Break
agenda.description: Stuck on Part 1 or 2? Grab the instructor now.

agenda.title: Round 3: Customers in Dollars
agenda.description: How many months does a customer stay? The matrix version of 1 ÷ (1 − r) answers it, and months times price gives lifetime value. Then a $2 decision with a plot twist.
bulletPoints: N = (I − Q)⁻¹: expected months in each state before churning
Lifetime value of a new customer: $193.17, the ceiling on acquisition cost
The $2 decision: lifting Active retention wins on gross value, but rescuing At-Risk customers wins once the cost is subtracted
Notebook Part 3 and the PageRank bonus: finish at home, they set up Homework #6

activities.title: From Transition Matrix to Customer Lifetime Value
activities.description: Build a complete customer-journey model for a $15/month subscription business: encode the transition matrix, project the customer base, find the steady state, and convert churn math into a defensible CLV number a CFO would accept.

steps.title: Part 1 · Where do customers go?
steps.description: Write the 4×4 table and check every row adds to 1. Move 10,000 Active customers forward one month with x @ P, then 36 months with a loop. Month 12 is the answer to the class vote.

steps.title: Part 2 · The long run
steps.description: Run a two-brand coffee market from three different starts and watch them meet at the steady state. Then count how long it takes everyone in the subscription chain to churn.

steps.title: Part 3 · Customers in dollars
steps.description: Compute N = (I − Q)⁻¹ for expected months in each state, turn months into lifetime value, and compare two $2-a-month campaigns on gain, cost, and net.

steps.title: Bonus · PageRank
steps.description: Build the random-surfer matrix for five pages and find the ranking with the same one line of code.

codeBlock.code:
import numpy as np

states = ["Active", "At-Risk", "Lapsed", "Churned"]
P = np.array([
    [0.80, 0.15, 0.03, 0.02],   # Active
    [0.30, 0.40, 0.20, 0.10],   # At-Risk
    [0.10, 0.10, 0.50, 0.30],   # Lapsed
    [0.00, 0.00, 0.00, 1.00],   # Churned (absorbing)
])

# Project 10,000 new customers 12 months forward
x = np.array([10_000.0, 0, 0, 0])
for _ in range(12):
    x = x @ P
print(dict(zip(states, x.round())))

# CLV via the fundamental matrix N = (I - Q)^-1
Q = P[:3, :3]                         # transient states only
N = np.linalg.inv(np.eye(3) - Q)      # expected months in each state
margin = np.array([15.0, 15.0, 0.0])  # $/month by state (Lapsed pays $0)
clv = N @ margin
print(f"CLV of a new Active customer: ${clv[0]:,.2f}")

activities.discussionNote: Your model says a new customer is worth $193.17, so that is the most you would pay to acquire one. Campaign A (keep Active customers happy) wins on gross value; campaign B (rescue At-Risk customers) wins once the $2 monthly cost is subtracted. Why? And what does that tell you about where to spend a retention budget?

takeaways.text: A transition matrix is a complete model of system dynamics in one object: multiply to project the future, find the eigenvector to see the long run, invert (I − Q) to price the journey. Customer bases, web surfers, and machine states all obey the same algebra.

Absorbing-chain math turns retention rates into dollars: customer lifetime value is expected time in paying states times margin — which is why small retention gains routinely beat big acquisition pushes.

Removal-effect attribution and PageRank are the same idea at different scales: measure a node's importance by what breaks when you take it out of the chain. Google turned that eigenvector into the modern web.
